title: Contains Duplicate
problem: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.
example: Explanation: 1 appears at index 0 and index 3.
intuition: The question is really "have I seen this value before?". If you check that question by scanning the array again every time, it costs O(n) per element. A hash set answers "seen before?" in O(1) on average, so you walk the array once, and the moment add fails you have found a duplicate.
Sorting is the middle ground: after sorting, equal values sit next to each other, so you only compare neighbours.
notes: Say it like this: "The brute force compares every pair in O(n²). Sorting brings duplicates together for O(n log n) with no extra memory. The optimal uses a HashSet: one pass, O(n) time, at the cost of O(n) space."
Edge cases: Empty array or single element (return false); negative numbers (fine with a set).
Common mistakes: Using JS default sort() without a comparator (sorts as strings); forgetting that sorting mutates the input.
Follow-ups: "What if memory is tight?" Sort in place, O(1) extra. "Duplicates within distance k?" (Contains Duplicate II) Keep a sliding-window set of the last k elements. 1.2
simple: You have a list of numbers. Is any number written twice? Think of a guest list where you want to know if someone signed in two times.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every index i, compare nums[i] with every nums[j] where j > i.
If any pair is equal, return true.
If no pair matches, return false.
approaches.why: We check all n(n-1)/2 pairs and use no extra structures.
approaches.simple: Take each number and compare it with every number after it. If any two match, you found a repeat. Simple, but slow for long lists.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Sort the array.
Duplicates are now adjacent; check nums[i] == nums[i-1] for every i.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the scan is O(n). Space is whatever the sort uses internally (it also modifies the input, mention that).
approaches.simple: Sort the list first. Equal numbers now sit side by side, so you only need to compare each number with its left neighbour.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Create an empty hash set.
For each number, try to add it. If it is already present, return true.
Return false after the loop.
approaches.why: Each insert/lookup is O(1) on average; in the worst case all n values go into the set.
approaches.simple: Keep a notebook (a set) of numbers you have already seen. For each new number, check the notebook first. If it is already there, that is the repeat.

title: Valid Anagram
problem: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, meaning it uses exactly the same characters with the same counts, possibly in a different order.
example: Explanation: Both have a×3, n×1, g×1, r×1, m×1.
intuition: Two strings are anagrams exactly when their character counts match. Order does not matter, only "how many of each letter". So either put both into a canonical order (sort them) or count the letters directly.
With only lowercase letters, a fixed int[26] counts faster than a hash map: add 1 for each char of s, subtract 1 for each char of t, and check everything ends at zero.
notes: Say it like this: "Sorting both strings and comparing is O(n log n). Since the alphabet is fixed, I count characters in an int[26], incrementing for s and decrementing for t, giving O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: Different lengths (early false); empty strings (true).
Common mistakes: Forgetting the length check; using two maps and comparing them clumsily.
Follow-ups: "What if the input has Unicode characters?" Use a HashMap<Character, Integer> (or Map in JS keyed by code point) instead of int[26]. 1.3
simple: Two words are anagrams if they use exactly the same letters the same number of times, like "listen" and "silent".

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: If lengths differ, return false.
Sort the characters of both strings.
Compare the sorted strings.
approaches.why: Sorting n characters dominates; we create char arrays of size n.
approaches.simple: Sort the letters of both words. If the sorted letters are identical, the words are anagrams.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: If lengths differ, return false.
Use count[26]: increment for each char of s, decrement for each char of t.
If any count is non-zero, return false; otherwise true.
approaches.why: One pass over both strings; the count array has a fixed 26 slots regardless of n.
approaches.simple: Keep 26 counters, one per letter. Add 1 for each letter of the first word and take away 1 for each letter of the second. If every counter ends at 0, the letters matched.

title: Two Sum
problem: Given an array nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one solution exists, and you may not use the same element twice.
intuition: For each number x, the partner you need is fixed: target - x. The brute force searches for that partner by scanning. The key observation is that you can remember every number you have already passed in a map value -> index. Then for the current x, "is target - x among the earlier numbers?" is an O(1) lookup.
Trace on [2,7,11,15], target 9: at 2, need 7, map is empty, store 2->0. At 7, need 2, map has it at index 0, answer [0,1].
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries every pair in O(n²). I can sort and use two pointers in O(n log n), but sorting loses the indices. The optimal is a single pass with a HashMap of value to index: for each number I look up target minus it, O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: Duplicate values like [3,3], target 6 (works because we check before inserting); negative numbers.
Common mistakes: Inserting before checking (pairs an element with itself when target = 2*x); returning values instead of indices.
Follow-ups: "Array is sorted?" (Two Sum II) Two pointers, O(1) space. "Return all unique pairs?" Sort + two pointers, skipping duplicates. "3Sum?" Fix one element, run Two Sum II on the rest. 1.4
simple: Find two numbers in the list that add up to the target and give back their positions.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each pair (i, j) with i < j, check if nums[i] + nums[j] == target.
Return [i, j] when found.
approaches.why: All pairs are checked; nothing extra is stored.
approaches.simple: Try every pair of numbers and check their sum. Stop when a pair hits the target.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Build pairs (value, originalIndex) and sort them by value.
Put left at the start and right at the end.
If the sum is too small move left right; if too big move right left; if equal, return both original indices.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; we need O(n) to remember original indices. This is the version to use if the question only asks "does a pair exist?" (then no index array is needed).
approaches.simple: Sort the numbers (remembering where each came from). Put one finger at the smallest and one at the largest. Too small? Move the left finger right. Too big? Move the right finger left.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep a map value -> index of numbers seen so far.
For each i, compute need = target - nums[i].
If need is in the map, return [map[need], i]; otherwise store nums[i] -> i.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) average map operations; the map can hold up to n entries.
approaches.simple: Walk through the list once. For each number, ask: "have I already seen the partner I need (target minus me)?" A map remembers every number you passed and where it was.

title: Group Anagrams
problem: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. Return the groups in any order.
example: Explanation: "eat","tea","ate" share the letters a,e,t; "tan","nat" share a,n,t.
intuition: All anagrams must map to the same "signature" and non-anagrams to different ones. Once you have such a signature, grouping is just Map<signature, List<String>>.

Two good signatures: the sorted string ("eat" -> "aet"), or the 26 letter counts written as a string ("eat" -> "1#0#0#0#1#...#1#..."). Sorting costs O(k log k) per word of length k; counting costs O(k).
notes: Say it like this: "I need a key that is identical for anagrams. Sorting each word gives O(n·k log k). Using the 26- letter count as the key removes the sort, so it is O(n·k) time and O(n·k) space for the map."
Edge cases: Empty string "" (forms its own group); single word; all words identical.

Common mistakes: Building the count key without separators (counts 1,11 and 11,1 would both become "111"); using char[] or int[] directly as a Java map key (arrays use identity equality, not content).
Follow-ups: "Huge alphabet / Unicode?" Sorted key is simpler then. "Very long words?" Count key is better because it avoids the log factor. 1.5
simple: Put words into groups so that each group holds words made of the same letters.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Keep a used[] flag per word.
For each unused word, start a new group and scan every later unused word; if it is an anagram (compare counts), add it and mark it used.
approaches.why: Each of the ~n²/2 pairs needs an O(k) anagram check; used[] is O(n) (output not counted).
approaches.simple: For each word, scan all the other words and pull out the ones that are anagrams of it. Lots of repeated comparing.

approaches.label: Better
steps: For each word, sort its characters to get a key.
Append the word to map[key].
Return all map values.
approaches.why: Each of n words is sorted in O(k log k); the map stores all characters.
approaches.simple: Sort the letters of each word to make a label ("eat" → "aet"). Words with the same label go into the same box in a map.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: For each word, count its letters into int[26].
Build a key from the counts with a separator, e.g. "1#0#0#...#".
Group by that key.
approaches.why: Counting is O(k) per word, and building the key is O(26) = O(1) extra per word. The map stores all words.
approaches.simple: Instead of sorting, count the letters of each word and use those 26 counts as the label. Same counts, same box.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. The answer is guaranteed to be unique; return it in any order.
example: Explanation: 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears 2 times, 3 appears once.
intuition: Step one is always the same: count frequencies with a hash map. The question is how to pick the top k from the counts.

Sort all distinct values by frequency: O(n log n). Keep a min-heap of size k: whenever it grows beyond k, pop the least frequent. O(n log k). Observe that a frequency is always between 1 and n. So make n+1 buckets where bucket[f] holds values with frequency f, then walk from the highest bucket down until you have k values. That is O(n), no comparison sort at all.
notes: Say it like this: "I count frequencies with a HashMap. Sorting by frequency is O(n log n); a size-k min-heap makes it O(n log k). Since frequencies are bounded by n, bucket sort by frequency gives O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: k equals the number of distinct values; all elements the same; negative numbers (fine, they are map keys, not indices).
Common mistakes: Using a max-heap of all elements (O(n log n), not better than sorting); bucket array of size n instead of n+1 (frequency n overflows).
Follow-ups: "Data is a stream?" Keep the size-k min-heap. "Top k frequent words with ties broken alphabetically?" Heap with a comparator on (count, word). 1.6
simple: Return the k numbers that show up most often.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Count frequencies in a map.
Sort the distinct values by frequency, descending.
Take the first k.
approaches.why: Up to n distinct values are sorted; the map and list hold up to n entries.
approaches.simple: Count how often each number appears, sort the numbers by that count, and take the first k.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Count frequencies.
Push each distinct value into a min-heap ordered by frequency.
If the heap size exceeds k, poll the smallest. The heap ends holding the top k.
approaches.why: Each of up to n distinct values costs one O(log k) heap operation. JS has no built-in heap, so in an interview you would usually say this approach and code bucket sort; a small heap is shown anyway.
approaches.simple: Count, then keep only a small group of k favourites in a min-heap. When the group gets too big, kick out the least frequent one.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Count frequencies.
Create bucket[0..n]; put each value into bucket[freq].
Walk buckets from n down to 1, collecting values until you have k.
approaches.why: Counting is O(n), filling buckets is O(distinct), and the backward walk touches n+1 buckets plus at most n values.
approaches.simple: Count, then drop each number into a bucket numbered by its count. Walk the buckets from the highest count down and pick numbers until you have k.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
problem: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings into a single string, and decode that string back into the original list. Strings may contain any character, including the ones you might want to use as a delimiter. (LeetCode 271, premium; also on NeetCode.)
intuition: The naive idea, "join with a comma", breaks the moment a string contains a comma. You need a format where the decoder never has to guess where a string ends.

Two classic fixes: escape the delimiter inside the strings (like CSV quoting), or prefix each string with its length. With a length prefix like 4#neet, the decoder reads digits up to #, gets 4, and then takes exactly 4 characters blindly, so the contents can contain # or digits safely.
notes: Say it like this: "A plain delimiter fails if a string contains it. I could escape the delimiter, but a length prefix is cleaner: each string becomes length#string, and the decoder reads the length and then jumps exactly that many characters. Both are O(total length)."
Edge cases: Empty list (encodes to "", decodes to []); empty strings ("0#"); strings containing # or digits; long strings with multi-digit lengths.
Common mistakes: Searching for the next # after the length instead of jumping by length (breaks when content has #); assuming the length is a single digit.

Follow-ups: "Binary-safe / fixed overhead?" Use a fixed 4-byte length header instead of digits + #. "Why not a rare Unicode char as delimiter?" It is still possible in input, so it is not guaranteed correct. 1.7
simple: Squash a list of words into one string, then split it back into the exact same words, even if the words contain tricky characters.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Inside each string, replace every # with ##.
End each string with the terminator #;.
To decode, scan: ## means a literal #; #; means the current string ends.
approaches.why: Each character is processed a constant number of times, but escaping can double the size of the encoded string.
approaches.simple: Mark the end of each word with a special pair of characters, and double any # inside a word so it can't be confused with the end mark.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Encode each string as length + "#" + string.
Decode with a pointer i: find the next # at j, parse len = s[i..j), take s[j+1.. j+1+len), set i = j+1+len.
approaches.why: Every character is read once; overhead is only a few characters per string, never a doubling.
approaches.simple: Write the length of each word before it, like "4#neet". When reading back, read the number, then grab exactly that many characters.

title: Product of Array Except Self
problem: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer where answer[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i]. You must not use division and must run in O(n).
intuition: answer[i] = (product of everything to the left of i) × (product of everything to the right of i). So if you know prefix products and suffix products, each answer is one multiplication.
To save memory, store the prefix products directly in the output array in a forward pass, then sweep backwards with a single running suffix variable and multiply it in.
Trace for [1,2,3,4]: prefix pass gives [1,1,2,6]. Backward with suffix = 1: i=3 → 6×1=6, suffix=4; i=2 → 2×4=8, suffix=12; i=1 → 1×12=12, suffix=24; i=0 → 1×24=24.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force multiplies everything except i for each i, O(n²). Each answer is left product times right product, so with prefix and suffix arrays it is O(n) time, O(n) space. I can store the prefix in the output and keep the suffix in one variable, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space."
Edge cases: One zero (only that index gets a non-zero product); two or more zeros (everything is 0); negative numbers.
Common mistakes: Using division (forbidden, and breaks on zeros); off-by-one in the prefix (must exclude nums[i] itself).
Follow-ups: "If division were allowed?" Total product / nums[i], but you must handle zeros by counting them. "Overflow?" LeetCode guarantees it fits in 32 bits; otherwise use long. 1.8
simple: For every position, find the product of all the other numbers, without using division.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each i, multiply all nums[j] with j!= i.
approaches.why: A full inner loop for each index; only the output array is allocated.
approaches.simple: For each position, multiply together all the other numbers. That repeats a lot of multiplication.

approaches.label: Better
steps: prefix[i] = product of nums[0..i-1] (with prefix[0] = 1).
suffix[i] = product of nums[i+1..n-1] (with suffix[n-1] = 1).
answer[i] = prefix[i] * suffix[i].
approaches.why: Three linear passes; two extra arrays of size n.
approaches.simple: Build two helper lists: the product of everything to the left of each spot, and everything to the right. Multiply the two for each spot.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Forward pass: ans[i] = product of everything left of i.
Backward pass with a running suffix = 1: ans[i] *= suffix, then suffix *= nums[i].
approaches.why: Two passes; the output array does not count as extra space by the problem's convention, and we only keep one variable.
approaches.simple: Same idea as Better but reuse the answer array: first fill it with left products, then sweep from the right keeping one running right product.

title: Valid Sudoku
pattern: Hash set / bitmask per row, column, box
problem: Given a 9×9 Sudoku board (digits '1' – '9' or '.' for empty), decide whether the filled cells are valid: no digit repeats in any row, any column, or any of the nine 3×3 boxes. The board does not need to be solvable.
example: Input:   a board whose first row is ["5","3",".",".","7",".",".",".","."], ... (LeetCode example 1)
Explanation: No row, column or 3×3 box contains a repeated digit.
intuition: There are 27 "units" (9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes) and each must have no duplicates. This is Contains Duplicate 27 times. The only trick is mapping a cell (r, c) to its box: box = (r / 3) * 3 + (c / 3), which numbers boxes 0..8 left to right, top to bottom.
You can check rows, columns and boxes in three separate passes, or do everything in one pass by keeping 27 sets (or 27 bitmasks of 9 bits).
notes: Say it like this: "Each of the 27 units must have no duplicates. I can check rows, columns and boxes in three passes with a set each. More cleanly, one pass with 27 bitmasks, using box index (r/3)*3 + c/3. Both are O(1) for a fixed 9×9 board, O(n²) for n×n."
Edge cases: Empty board (valid); a board that is valid but unsolvable (still true).
Common mistakes: Wrong box formula (r/3 + c/3 collides); forgetting to skip '.'; in JS forgetting Math.floor for the box index.
Follow-ups: "Now solve the Sudoku." Backtracking with the same row/col/box masks to test placements in O(1) (Sudoku Solver, LeetCode 37). 1.9
simple: Check a partly filled Sudoku: no digit may repeat in any row, column, or 3×3 box.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each row, use a fresh set to check duplicates.
Repeat for each column.
Repeat for each 3×3 box.
approaches.why: The board is fixed at 81 cells; we scan it three times. For a general n×n board this is O(n²) time and O(n) space.
approaches.simple: Check every row with a fresh set, then every column, then every box. If any set sees a digit twice, the board is invalid.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep three arrays of 9 bitmasks: rows, cols, boxes.
For each filled cell with digit d, let bit = 1 << d and b = (r/3)*3 + c/3.
If bit is already set in rows[r], cols[c] or boxes[b], return false; otherwise set it in all three.
approaches.why: One pass over the board; 27 integers of state. Same Big-O as the brute force, but a single pass and no set objects, which is what interviewers expect.
approaches.simple: One pass over the board. For each digit, flip a bit in its row, column and box records. If the bit is already on, that digit is repeated.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problem: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like 1,2,3,4) that can be formed from its elements. The elements do not need to be adjacent in the array. Required time: O(n).
example: Explanation: The longest consecutive run is 1, 2, 3, 4.
intuition: If you sort, consecutive values line up and one scan finds the longest run, but that is O(n log n). To get O(n), put everything in a hash set so "does x+1 exist?" is O(1).

The trap: if you start counting upward from every number, a run of length L is re-counted from each of its L elements, which is O(n²) in the worst case. The fix is the key observation of this problem: only start counting from x if x - 1 is not in the set. Then x is the true start of its run, and every run is walked exactly once.
Trace on {100,4,200,1,3,2}: 100 (99 missing) → run length 1. 4 (3 present) → skip. 200 → 1. 1 (0 missing) → count 1,2,3,4 → 4. 3, 2 → skip. Answer 4.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force walks upward from each number with linear searches. Sorting gives O(n log n). For O(n), I put everything in a HashSet and only start counting from numbers whose predecessor is missing, so each run is walked once: O(n) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: Empty array (0); duplicates like [1,2,2,3] (answer 3); negative numbers; Integer.MAX_VALUE (in Java x + len can overflow; LeetCode limits are ±1e9, so it is safe there).
Common mistakes: Iterating over nums instead of the set (with many duplicates of a run start, the run is re- walked each time and can degrade to O(n²)); forgetting the x - 1 check.
Follow-ups: "Return the sequence itself?" Remember the start and length of the best run. "Streaming inserts?" Union-Find or a map of run boundaries (merge neighbouring runs on insert). 1.10
simple: Find the longest run of numbers that follow one another (like 1, 2, 3, 4), in any order in the list.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each element x, set cur = x, len = 1.
While cur + 1 exists in the array (found by a linear scan), increment cur and len.
Track the maximum len.
approaches.why: Up to n starting points, each run can be up to n long, and each "exists?" check is an O(n) scan. (Many sources loosely call this O(n²); the honest worst case for [1..n] is cubic.)
approaches.simple: From each number, keep looking for the next number up by scanning the whole list again. Very slow.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Sort the array.
Scan, keeping lastSmaller (previous distinct value) and cur (current run length).
If nums[i] == lastSmaller + 1, extend the run; if equal to lastSmaller, skip the duplicate; otherwise reset cur = 1.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the scan is O(n). Sorting mutates the input.
approaches.simple: Sort the list, then walk it counting how long each run of +1 steps is. Skip duplicates.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Insert all numbers into a hash set.
For each x in the set, if x - 1 is not in the set, x starts a run: count x, x+1, x+2,... while present.
Track the maximum length.
approaches.why: Building the set is O(n). Each number is visited once by the outer loop and at most once more inside the while loop (only from its run's start), so total work is O(n).
approaches.simple: Put all numbers in a set. Only start counting from a number whose smaller neighbour is missing (the start of a run), then count upward while the next number exists.

title: Majority Element-I
problem: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element: the one that appears more than n/2 times. It is guaranteed to exist.
example: Explanation: 2 appears 4 times, which is more than 7/2 = 3.5.
intuition: Counting with a hash map works but uses O(n) space. The clever O(1)-space idea is cancellation: pair each majority vote with a different vote and cancel both. Because the majority has more than half the votes, it cannot be fully cancelled, so it is what survives.
Moore's voting does this on the fly: keep a candidate and a count. Same value → count++; different value → count--; when count hits 0, the next element becomes the new candidate.
notes: Say it like this: "Counting each element is O(n²); a HashMap makes it O(n) time but O(n) space. Boyer-Moore voting cancels each majority vote against a different one; since the majority has more than half, it survives. O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: Single element; all elements equal; if the majority is not guaranteed, verify with a second counting pass.
Common mistakes: Returning the candidate without verification when existence is not guaranteed; using >= n/2 instead of > n/2.
Follow-ups: "Elements appearing more than n/3 times?" Majority Element II, next question: two candidates. Sorting also works: the majority is always at index n/2 (O(n log n)). 1.11
simple: Find the number that appears more than half the time.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each element, count how many times it appears by scanning the array.
Return it as soon as its count exceeds n/2.
approaches.why: An O(n) count for each of n elements.
approaches.simple: For each number, count how many times it appears by scanning everything.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Count every value in a hash map.
Return the value whose count exceeds n/2.
approaches.why: One pass to count; the map can hold up to about n/2 distinct keys.
approaches.simple: Count every number in a map and return the one whose count passes n/2.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: candidate = none, count = 0.
For each x: if count == 0, set candidate = x. Then count += (x == candidate)? 1: -1.
Return candidate (if existence were not guaranteed, do a second pass to verify its count).
approaches.why: A single pass with two variables.
approaches.simple: Voting: keep one candidate and a score. Same number adds a vote, a different one removes a vote. When the score hits 0, pick a new candidate. The majority always survives.

title: Majority Element-II
problem: Given an integer array nums of size n, return all elements that appear more than ⌊n/3⌋ times, in any order.
example: Explanation: n = 8, n/3 = 2. Both 1 and 2 appear 3 times; 3 appears only twice.
intuition: How many elements can appear more than n/3 times? At most two, because three of them would need more than n elements in total. So the answer list has size 0, 1 or 2.

Extend Moore's voting to two candidates. When a new element matches neither candidate and both counts are positive, decrement both: that cancels a triple of three distinct values. Anything appearing more than n/3 times cannot be fully cancelled this way. The survivors are only candidates, so a second pass must verify their real counts.
notes: Say it like this: "At most two elements can exceed n/3. Brute force counts each in O(n²); a HashMap does O(n) time and space. Extended Boyer-Moore keeps two candidates and cancels triples of distinct values, then a second pass verifies them: O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: All elements equal (only one answer; the else if in the verify pass prevents adding it twice); n < 3; no element qualifies (empty list).

Common mistakes: Skipping the verification pass (candidates are not guaranteed answers); checking cnt1 == 0 before checking x == c2 (then the same value can occupy both slots); missing the cnt > 0 guard when comparing with stale candidates.
Follow-ups: "Generalise to more than n/k?" Keep k-1 candidates in a map (Misra-Gries), O(n·k) time and O(k) space. 1.12
simple: Find every number that appears more than n/3 times. There can be at most two.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each element not already in the answer, count its occurrences.
If the count exceeds n/3, add it. Stop once the answer has 2 elements.
approaches.why: Counting each element is O(n); the answer list has at most 2 items.
approaches.simple: Count each number by scanning, and keep the ones above n/3.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Count with a hash map.
Add an element to the answer the moment its count becomes exactly ⌊n/3⌋ + 1 (so it is added once).
approaches.why: One pass; the map can hold up to n distinct keys.
approaches.simple: Count with a map and add a number to the answer the moment its count passes n/3.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep (c1, cnt1) and (c2, cnt2).
For each x: if x == c1, cnt1++; else if x == c2, cnt2++; else if cnt1 == 0, take c1 = x, cnt1 = 1; else if cnt2 == 0, take c2 = x, cnt2 = 1; else decrement both counts.
Second pass: count real occurrences of c1 and c2, keep those above n/3 (and don't add the same value twice).
approaches.why: Two linear passes with four variables.
approaches.simple: Voting with two candidates and two scores. A number that matches neither candidate removes a vote from both. Then double-check the two survivors with a real count.

title: Count Inversions
problem: Given an array of integers, count the number of inversions: pairs (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > a[j]. The count tells you how far the array is from sorted. (GFG / Striver problem; not on LeetCode. Signature assumed: long numberOfInversions(int[] nums).)
intuition: Brute force checks every pair: O(n²). To do better, think about merge sort. When you merge two sorted halves left and right, every element of left was originally before every element of right. If left[i] > right[j], then because left is sorted, every element from left[i] to the end of left is also greater than right[j]. That is mid - i + 1 inversions found in one step instead of one by one.
So: count inversions inside the left half (recursively), inside the right half (recursively), and across the halves (during merge). Total cost is the cost of merge sort.
Small trace: merging [3,5] and [1,2,4]. 3 > 1 → both 3 and 5 beat 1: +2. 3 > 2 → +2. 3 < 4 → take 3. 5 > 4 → +1. Cross inversions = 5.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force counts all pairs in O(n²). During merge sort, when a right-half element is smaller than left[i], it is smaller than everything from i to mid because the left half is sorted, so I add mid - i + 1 at once. That gives O(n log n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: Sorted array (0); reverse sorted (n(n-1)/2, needs long); duplicates (equal elements are not inversions, so use <= when taking from the left).
Common mistakes: Using int for the count; using < instead of <= (counts equal pairs as inversions); adding mid - i instead of mid - i + 1.

Follow-ups: "Another way?" A Fenwick tree (BIT) over compressed values: scan right to left, query how many smaller values were seen, O(n log n). "Reverse Pairs?" Same skeleton with a different condition (next question). 1.13
simple: Count pairs where a bigger number appears before a smaller one.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each pair i < j, if a[i] > a[j], increment the count.
approaches.why: All pairs are checked. Use long for the count, since it can reach n(n-1)/2 ≈ 5×10⁹ for n = 10⁵, which overflows int.
approaches.simple: Check every pair (i before j) and count when the left one is bigger.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Recursively merge sort [low, mid] and [mid+1, high], adding the inversions each half returns.
While merging with pointers i (left) and j (right): if a[i] <= a[j], take a[i]; else take a[j] and add mid - i + 1.
Copy the merged result back.
approaches.why: Standard merge sort: log n levels, O(n) merge work per level. The temp buffer is O(n), plus O(log n) recursion stack. It sorts (modifies) the input, so copy it first if the caller needs the original.
approaches.simple: Use merge sort. When an item from the right half is placed before items still waiting in the left half, each of those left items forms a pair with it, so count them all at once.

title: Reverse Pairs
problem: Given an integer array nums, return the number of reverse pairs: pairs (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j].
example: Explanation: (3 at index 1, 1 at index 4) and (3 at index 3, 1 at index 4): 3 > 2*1.
intuition: This looks like Count Inversions with a different condition, and the same merge-sort idea works, with one important twist. In Count Inversions we counted while merging, because the comparison for counting (a[i] > a[j]) was the same comparison used for merging. Here the counting condition is a[i] > 2*a[j], which is different from the merge order. So you count in a separate pass before merging.

Since both halves are sorted, use two pointers: for each i in the left half, move j forward in the right half while a[i] > 2*a[j]. As i increases, a[i] only grows, so j never needs to move back. That pass is O(n) per merge, and then you merge normally.
Watch out: 2 * nums[j] overflows int when nums[j] is near ±2³¹. Use 2L * nums[j] in Java.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force is O(n²). I use merge sort: after both halves are sorted, a two-pointer pass counts, for each left element, how many right elements satisfy a[i] > 2·a[j], and the pointer never moves back. Then I merge normally. O(n log n) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: Negative numbers (-5 > 2*-3 is true, the sorted two-pointer logic still holds); values near Integer.MAX_VALUE (overflow); single element.
Common mistakes: Counting inside the merge loop like Count Inversions (wrong, the conditions differ); 2 * a[j] in int overflowing; resetting j for each i (makes the pass O(n²)).

Follow-ups: "Alternative?" BIT / segment tree on coordinate-compressed values including 2*x, O(n log n). "Count of smaller numbers after self (LC 315)?" Same merge-sort family, but you track original indices. 1.14
simple: Count pairs i < j where nums[i] is more than twice nums[j].

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every pair i < j, check nums[i] > 2L * nums[j].
approaches.why: All pairs are checked. Times out for n = 5×10⁴ on LeetCode.
approaches.simple: Check every pair and count the ones that pass the test.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Merge sort recursively; add counts from both halves.
Before merging, with sorted halves [low..mid] and [mid+1..high]: set j = mid+1; for each i from low to mid, advance j while j <= high && a[i] > 2L*a[j]; add j - (mid+1).
Merge the halves normally.
approaches.why: Each level of recursion does an O(n) counting pass plus an O(n) merge; there are log n levels. Temp buffer O(n).
approaches.simple: Merge sort again. Before merging two sorted halves, slide a pointer through the right half to count, for each left item, how many right items are small enough.

title: Longest subarray with sum K
pattern: Prefix sum + hash map / Sliding window (non-negatives)
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose sum equals k, or 0 if none exists. Striver's sheet has two versions: array with only positives (and zeros), and array that may contain negatives. LeetCode 325 "Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k" (premium) is the negatives version; its signature is used below.
example: Explanation: [5, 2, 7, 1] sums to 15 and is the longest such subarray.
intuition: Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements. The sum of subarray (j, i] is prefix[i] - prefix[j]. We want it to equal k, i.e. we want an earlier prefix equal to prefix[i] - k. To make the subarray as long as possible, we want the earliest such j. So store each prefix sum the first time it appears, in a map prefixSum -> firstIndex. This works for any integers, including negatives.

If all numbers are non-negative, there is an even leaner idea: a sliding window. Extending the window to the right never decreases the sum, and shrinking from the left never increases it. So if the window sum exceeds k, shrink from the left; if it equals k, record the length. This needs O(1) space. It breaks with negatives, because then shrinking might increase the sum, so the window can't decide which way to move.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force tries every subarray with a running sum, O(n²). With prefix sums, a subarray ending at i sums to k when an earlier prefix equals prefix − k; storing the earliest index of each prefix gives O(n) time and O(n) space, and it handles negatives. If all numbers are non-negative, a sliding window does it in O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: No valid subarray (0); the whole array; zeros in the array (putIfAbsent keeps the earliest index so zeros extend the length); k = 0.

Common mistakes: Overwriting the map with later indices (gives shorter answers); forgetting the 0 -> -1 entry (misses subarrays starting at index 0); using the sliding window when negatives are allowed.

Follow-ups: "Count such subarrays instead of the longest?" Store counts instead of first indices (next question). "Longest subarray with sum ≤ k (non-negatives)?" Same sliding window, record length whenever sum <= k. 1.15
simple: Find the longest stretch of neighbours whose sum is exactly k.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i, keep a running sum while extending the end j.
Whenever the sum equals k, update the best length with j - i + 1.
approaches.why: Every (start, end) pair is visited once; the running sum avoids a third loop.
approaches.simple: Try every start point and keep adding to the right, remembering the longest stretch that hits k.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: (This is the optimal solution when the array can contain negatives, i.e. the LeetCode 325 version.)
steps: Map firstIndex with 0 -> -1 (empty prefix before index 0).
Walk the array keeping prefix. If prefix - k is in the map, update best with i - firstIndex[prefix - k].
Store prefix -> i only if prefix is not already in the map (keep the earliest index).
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) average map operations; up to n distinct prefix sums are stored.
approaches.simple: Keep a running total and a map of where each total first appeared. If the total minus k appeared before, the stretch in between sums to k.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: (Only valid when all elements are non-negative, Striver's "positives" version.)
steps: Keep a window [left, right] and its sum.
Add nums[right] to sum. While sum > k and left <= right, subtract nums[left] and move left right.
If sum == k, update best with right - left + 1.
approaches.why: right moves n times and left moves at most n times in total, so the work is O(2n).
approaches.simple: With non-negative numbers, use a sliding window: grow on the right, shrink from the left while the sum is too big, and record the length whenever the sum equals k.

title: Count subarrays with given sum
problem: Given an integer array nums (may contain negatives) and an integer k, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k. (LeetCode 560, Subarray Sum Equals K.)
intuition: Same prefix-sum identity as the previous question: subarray (j, i] sums to k exactly when prefix[j] = prefix[i] - k. Now we want how many such j exist, not the earliest one. So store a map prefixSum -> how many times it has occurred so far. At each index, add count[prefix - k] to the answer, then record the current prefix.
Seed the map with {0: 1}: the empty prefix, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.
Trace [1,2,3], k=3: prefixes 1, 3, 6. At prefix 1: need -2, none. At 3: need 0, count 1 → total 1. At 6: need 3, count 1 → total 2.
Because of negatives, a sliding window does not work here; the map is the real solution.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force sums every subarray with a running total, O(n²). A subarray ending at i sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals prefix − k, so I keep a HashMap of prefix-sum frequencies and add the matching count at each step. O(n) time, O(n) space."
Edge cases: k = 0 (the {0:1} seed plus updating after counting keeps it correct); negative numbers; all zeros with k = 0 (n(n+1)/2 subarrays).
Common mistakes: Forgetting freq.put(0, 1); updating the map before reading it (counts the empty subarray when k = 0); trying a sliding window (fails with negatives).

Follow-ups: "Subarrays with sum divisible by k (LC 974)?" Same idea with prefix mod k as the key (normalise negative remainders). "Binary array, count subarrays with sum = goal?" Same map, or atMost(goal) − atMost(goal−1) sliding windows. 1.16
simple: Count how many stretches of neighbours add up to exactly k.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each start i, extend j with a running sum.
Every time the sum equals k, increment the count.
approaches.why: All (i, j) pairs; running sum makes each O(1). (The even more naive version recomputes each sum with a third loop for O(n³).)
approaches.simple: Try every start and every end with a running sum and count the hits.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: freq = {0: 1}, prefix = 0, count = 0.
For each number: prefix += x; count += freq[prefix - k] (0 if absent); freq[prefix]++.
Return count.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) average map operations; up to n+1 distinct prefixes are stored.
approaches.simple: Keep a running total. A stretch sums to k when an earlier running total equals (current total − k). A map counts how many times each total has appeared.

title: Count subarrays with given xor K
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose bitwise XOR of all elements equals k. (GFG / Striver problem, "Subarrays with XOR K"; signature assumed: long subarraysWithXorK(int[] nums, int k).)
intuition: This is the previous problem with XOR instead of addition. Define px[i] = XOR of the first i elements. XOR of subarray (j, i] is px[i] ^ px[j] (the common prefix cancels itself because a ^ a = 0). We want px[i] ^ px[j] = k, which rearranges to px[j] = px[i] ^ k (XOR both sides with px[i]; XOR is its own inverse).
So keep a map prefixXor -> frequency, seed with {0: 1}, and at each index add freq[px ^ k].
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force keeps a running XOR for every start, O(n²). Since XOR of a subarray is prefixXor[i] ^ prefixXor[j], I need earlier prefixes equal to current ^ k; a HashMap of prefix-XOR frequencies gives O(n) time and O(n) space. It's exactly the subarray-sum-K template with ^ in place of +/−."
Edge cases: k = 0 (counts subarrays whose XOR cancels out, the {0:1} seed handles prefixes); single element equal to k; large counts (use long).
Common mistakes: Looking up xr - k (sum habit) instead of xr ^ k; forgetting the {0:1} seed; trying a sliding window (XOR is not monotonic).

Follow-ups: "Maximum XOR of any subarray?" Prefix XORs inserted into a binary trie, query best partner per prefix, O(n · 32). "Longest subarray with XOR k?" Store first index of each prefix XOR instead of a count (same as 1.14).
simple: Count how many stretches of neighbours have XOR equal to k.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each start i, extend j keeping a running XOR.
Count every time the running XOR equals k.
approaches.why: All (i, j) pairs with O(1) work each. The count can reach n(n+1)/2, which overflows int for n near 10⁵, so we return long.
approaches.simple: Try every start and end, keeping a running XOR, and count the hits.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: freq = {0: 1}, xr = 0, count = 0.
For each number: xr ^= x; count += freq[xr ^ k]; freq[xr]++.
Return count.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) average map operations; up to n+1 distinct prefix XORs.
approaches.simple: Same trick as prefix sums but with XOR: a stretch has XOR k when an earlier running XOR equals (current XOR ^ k). Count earlier XORs in a map.
